name: Kota Kinabalu International Airport
before:
Sabah's airport and the primary gateway to East Malaysia, about 8 km south west of Kota Kinabalu. It is the second busiest in the country after Kuala Lumpur, handling more than 7.95 million passengers in 2024, and third for cargo.

It is the main hub for MASwings, AirAsia Malaysia's second largest base after KLIA2, and a secondary hub for Firefly and Malaysia Airlines, so connections onward into Borneo are good.

Terminal 1 is the main building and it is a generous one: 64 check in counters, 36 immigration positions, six baggage carousels, twelve air bridges and 1,400 parking spaces, rated for nine million passengers a year across five floors.

It is also one of the better looking terminals in the region. The column heads in the departure hall take their shape from the wakid, the Sabahan carrying basket that traditionally stands for setting out on a journey that matters, and the floor tiles carry Rungus and Bajau patterns.
after: Sabah's main airport, about 8 km south west of Kota Kinabalu. It is the second busiest in Malaysia after Kuala Lumpur, and the transport ministry's quarterly figures add up to about 8.9 million passengers in 2025.

claims.note: Was 'Sabah's airport and the primary gateway to East Malaysia'. The ministry's fourth-quarter 2025 table puts Kota Kinabalu at 2,151,556 of the 3,208,618 passengers through Sabah's airports that quarter, far ahead of Tawau and Sandakan; Wikipedia calls it the airport of Sabah's state capital. 'Primary gateway to East Malaysia' is Wikipedia's alone.

claims.note: Replaces 'more than 7.95 million passengers in 2024': a passenger total replaces a passenger total. The ministry's four 2025 tables give 2,195,169, 2,210,642, 2,323,652 and 2,151,556, which add up to 8,881,019 (the table credits Malaysia Airports as its source). The same sum for 2024 gives 7,954,338, exactly Wikipedia's infobox figure, which ties the tables to independent reporting; the 2025 total is the ministry's, attributed.

claims.claim: the primary gateway to East Malaysia
claims.wasBefore: Sabah's airport and the primary gateway to East Malaysia
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. Reworded to Sabah's main airport, which the ministry's figures show (see above).

claims.claim: more than 7.95 million passengers in 2024; third for cargo
claims.wasBefore: It is the second busiest in the country after Kuala Lumpur, handling more than 7.95 million passengers in 2024, and third for cargo.
claims.why: The 2024 total is confirmed (the ministry's quarters add up to 7,954,338) but superseded by 2025 (see above). 'Third for cargo' needs a full-year cargo table, and only the ministry's fourth-quarter 2025 cargo table was saved.

claims.claim: main hub for MASwings; AirAsia Malaysia's second largest base; secondary hub for Firefly and Malaysia Airlines
claims.wasBefore: It is the main hub for MASwings, AirAsia Malaysia's second largest base after KLIA2, and a secondary hub for Firefly and Malaysia Airlines, so connections onward into Borneo are good.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The operator's airport page is built by script and its saved copy showed another airport's page; no airline page naming its bases was read. Worth restoring with the airlines' own pages (MASwings' ownership has been changing, so it needs a current source).

claims.claim: Terminal 1's counters, immigration, carousels, air bridges, parking and 9 million capacity
claims.wasBefore: Terminal 1 is the main building and it is a generous one: 64 check in counters, 36 immigration positions, six baggage carousels, twelve air bridges and 1,400 parking spaces, rated for nine million passengers a year across five floors.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone (see above). Its 2025 traffic, 8.9 million, is already close to the nine million the old text gave as the terminal's rating.

claims.claim: the wakid column heads and Rungus and Bajau floor patterns
claims.wasBefore: It is also one of the better looking terminals in the region. The column heads in the departure hall take their shape from the wakid, the Sabahan carrying basket that traditionally stands for setting out on a journey that matters, and the floor tiles carry Rungus and Bajau patterns.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone; nothing else read describes the terminal.
